sections.h2: What happens before a Pennsylvania sheriff sale can be held?
sections.html:
No sheriff sale of real property can go forward until the plaintiff files an affidavit with the sheriff and the required notice has been served. Pa.R.C.P. 3129.1 sets that rule, and it applies to a sale held on a writ of execution after a judgment.

The affidavit lists, as best the plaintiff knows, the owner or reputed owner, the defendant in the judgment, every person holding a record lien, and anyone with a record interest the sale could affect. It also names people with an unrecorded interest of which the plaintiff has knowledge. If an address cannot be found, the affidavit says so.

sections.h2: What notices must an owner receive?
sections.html:
Three separate notices precede the sale: handbills, written notice and newspaper publication. Pa.R.C.P. 3129.2 sets the timing for each one.

Notice of sale of real property, summarized from Pa.R.C.P. 3129.2
NoticeWho gives itTiming
HandbillsSheriff, posted at the sheriff's office and on the propertyAt least 30 days before the sale
Written noticePlaintiff, to everyone named in the affidavitServed at least 30 days before the sale
Newspaper publicationSheriff, once a week for three weeksFirst notice at least 21 days before the sale

Each handbill describes the property and its improvements, the judgment, the owner's name, and the time and place of the sale. It also tells claimants that the sheriff will file a schedule of distribution within 30 days after the sale, and that objections to it are due within ten days of filing.

sections.h2: How is the written notice delivered?
sections.html:
The method depends on who the recipient is. The plaintiff prepares the notice, and the rule allows several routes.

  • An owner or a defendant who has not appeared in the case: service by the sheriff or a competent adult, or by the plaintiff mailing a copy under Rule 403.
  • A defendant who has appeared: service by the plaintiff under Rule 440.
  • Other people named in the affidavit: ordinary mail from the plaintiff, backed by a USPS Form 3817 certificate of mailing. Service is complete on mailing, and returned mail does not undo it.
  • If neither personal service nor mailing works: service under a special court order.

Whoever serves the notice files a return of service. When service reaches a person fewer than 30 days before the date, the notice counts as timely only if the sale is continued to a date at least 30 days after the last required service.

sections.h2: What is an Act 91 notice, and what is HEMAP?
sections.html:
Act 91 of 1983 created the Homeowners' Emergency Mortgage Assistance Program, run by the Pennsylvania Housing Finance Agency. It is a loan program for owners facing foreclosure through no fault of their own. It is not a grant, and the funds must be repaid.

  • The home must be in Pennsylvania, owner-occupied, and a one- or two-family residence.
  • The owner must be at least 60 days behind and must have received an Act 91 Notice from the lender.
  • FHA Title II purchase mortgages are not eligible.
  • A loan is capped at 24 or 36 months of delinquency or $60,000, whichever comes first.
  • The minimum monthly payment set by law is $25 per mortgage assisted.

The clock is short. A face-to-face meeting with an approved counseling agency must happen within 33 days of the notice date, the agency must send the application to PHFA within 30 days of that meeting, and PHFA decides within 60 days of receiving it. Foreclosure actions pause while those time limits are met. The counselor will ask for a letter explaining the hardship, the Act 91 Notice, photo identification, three recent pay stubs, three years of federal tax returns, the deed, and monthly statements for loans and charge accounts. A denial can be appealed in writing, postmarked within 15 days of the denial letter. The HEMAP office is at 717-780-3940 or 1-800-342-2397.

sections.h2: Can a court set aside the sale?
sections.html:
Yes, but only on a petition filed in time. Rule 3132 lets the court, on petition of a party in interest and for proper cause, set aside the sale and order a resale before the sheriff's deed is delivered.

The sheriff executes the deed no sooner than 20 days and no later than 40 days after the schedule of distribution is filed, or after the sale if no schedule is needed, provided no petition to set the sale aside is pending. Rule 3135 also lets a purchaser ask the court to correct a defective deed, and it gives a plaintiff or purchaser a path to divest a junior lienholder who never received notice.

sections.h2: Does the sale wipe out what I owe?
sections.html:
Not always. When the lender buys the house at the sale for less than the judgment, 42 Pa.C.S. 8103 requires the lender to petition the court to fix the property's fair market value before collecting any balance. The debtor is then released to the extent of that value, less prior liens, costs and taxes not discharged by the sale.

If the lender fails to file within the six-month period in section 5522, the debtor or another person bound by the judgment may petition to have the judgment marked satisfied. The statute also voids any agreement to waive these protections. A debtor or owner who was never named or served in the valuation petition is discharged from personal liability on that debt.

sections.h2: Who is paid from the sale proceeds?
sections.html:
The sheriff files a schedule of distribution that shows how the money will be split among the parties with claims. Under the handbill language in Rule 3129.2, that schedule is filed no later than 30 days after the sale, and distribution follows it unless someone files exceptions within ten days after filing.

That ten-day window matters to owners with surplus money, to junior lienholders and to anyone else who thinks the numbers are wrong. Check the sheriff's office for the filing date, since the handbill states the date the sheriff chose.

sections.h2: Is transfer tax due on a foreclosure sale?
sections.html: Generally no. Under 61 Pa. Code 91.193, transfers made under a mortgage foreclosure action, and transfers in a judicial sale for tax collection, are excluded from realty transfer tax. So is a deed in lieu of foreclosure to the mortgage holder, if the statement of value shows where the mortgage is recorded. The deed-in-lieu exclusion does not extend to someone who buys or is assigned the lender's bid.

sections.h2: Can I sell the house before the sheriff sale date?
sections.html:
Yes, an owner can sell before the sale takes place, and a closing that pays the lender in full removes the reason for the sale. Ask the lender or its attorney for a written payoff figure that includes legal costs, and give your buyer's title company that number so the closing date stays ahead of the sheriff's date.

Check the handbill and the written notice for the exact date. A sale can be continued, so confirm the current date with the county sheriff's office before you commit to a closing schedule. The county's Prothonotary or sheriff can tell you where the case stands.

faqs.q: How much notice does an owner get before a sheriff sale?
faqs.a: At least 30 days. The sheriff posts handbills 30 days ahead, the plaintiff serves written notice 30 days ahead, and newspaper publication starts at least 21 days before the sale.

faqs.q: Can the lender and I still work something out after the notice?
faqs.a: Yes. HEMAP exists for exactly this, and an application started within the 33-day window pauses the foreclosure while the time limits are met. Ask your lender about other options too.

faqs.q: How long after the sale is the sheriff's deed delivered?
faqs.a: The sheriff delivers the deed no sooner than 20 days and no later than 40 days after the schedule of distribution or the sale, unless a petition to set the sale aside has been filed.

faqs.q: Can a lender chase me for money after the sale?
faqs.a: Only after it petitions the court to fix fair market value under 42 Pa.C.S. 8103. You are credited with that value against the debt, and if the lender misses the six-month deadline you may ask the court to mark the judgment satisfied.
The county sheriff. The sheriff of the county where the property sits posts the handbills and publishes the notice of sale.
